post.title: Code is not just context. It is the primary signal.
post.content:
Semantic search has spent years perfecting the art of reading prose.

It turns out that reading the prose is the easy part. The hard part is
understanding that in software engineering, the text is often just a
noisy wrapper around the actual intent. A user describes a problem in
natural language, but the logic is trapped in the syntax of the snippet.

If a search engine only looks at the description, it is blind to the
structural reality of the bug or the implementation.

Jan Pašek and colleagues address this with MQDD multimodal duplicate
detection. The model does not just parse the question. It treats the
question descriptions and the source code across multiple programming
languages as a unified input. It uses two new learning objectives to
bridge the gap between how humans talk about code and how code actually
behaves.

This shifts the burden of relevance from the linguist to the compiler.

When duplicate detection becomes multimodal, the traditional hierarchy
of information breaks. We have spent decades optimizing indexing for
keywords and embeddings of English sentences. But a keyword match on
"how to sort a list" is useless if the code snippet shows a specific
edge case in a custom object implementation.

The downstream consequence is a change in how we curate technical
knowledge. If the model can see the code, the "correctness" of a
duplicate flag no longer depends on how well a user writes their
paragraph. It depends on the structural overlap of the logic.

This makes the Stack Overflow Dataset (SOD) and the Stack Overflow
Duplicity Dataset (SODD) more than just training sets. They are
benchmarks for a new kind of retrieval. They force us to admit that
a search system that cannot parse a loop is not a technical search
system at all. It is just a glorified forum index.

We are moving toward a world where the prose is the secondary signal,
and the code is the ground truth.


## Sources
